analysis.one_liner: Removes Medicare's 190-day lifetime cap on inpatient psychiatric hospital care.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare is the only part of American health insurance with a lifetime limit on inpatient psychiatric hospital care: 190 days over a person's entire life. Once a beneficiary hits that cap, Medicare stops paying for psychiatric hospital stays, no matter how severe the illness. This bill would delete that limit, effective January 1, 2023, so Medicare coverage for inpatient psychiatric care would work like its coverage for other hospital care.
analysis.who_benefits: Older and disabled people with Medicare who have severe mental illness and need longer-term psychiatric hospitalization, along with their families, who currently face the 190-day lifetime cap and then must pay out of pocket, rely on general hospital units, or go without care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients with serious mental illness

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the 190-day lifetime limit on inpatient psychiatric hospital services under Medicare, the only lifetime cap of its kind in the program.
The change would apply to items and services furnished on or after January 1, 2023.
After the limit, Medicare pays nothing toward psychiatric hospital stays; removing the cap lets coverage continue like coverage for other hospital care.

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program and taxpayers, through higher federal spending on extended inpatient psychiatric stays, plus some cost-sharing by beneficiaries who use far more than 190 lifetime days.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Medicare trust fund and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Removing the cap means open-ended federal Medicare spending on psychiatric hospitalization, a cost the 190-day limit was designed to contain.

A good-faith objection is that guaranteeing long-term inpatient coverage could pull resources and patients toward institutional psychiatric care rather than community-based mental health treatment, a concern historically behind Medicare's limits on psychiatric facilities; the bill does not address that trade-off.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and well-targeted but narrow: it protects a small group of very ill Medicare beneficiaries from catastrophic out-of-pocket costs once they exhaust 190 lifetime days. The cost is higher Medicare spending with no offset, and the bill does not address whether long-term institutional care is the best use of those dollars versus community-based treatment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and its Health Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on October 21, 2021, joined by Rep. Bill Huizenga.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to its Subcommittee on Health the same day.
No further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the 117th Congress.
The bill would have removed the 190-day lifetime limit on inpatient psychiatric hospital services under Medicare.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained ground: the status quo holds, so Medicare keeps the 190-day lifetime cap and the federal government continues to limit its psychiatric hospital spending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: Medicare keeps the 190-day cap

for.role: Original and additional cosponsors, including Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-MI)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 21, 2021, and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor picked up three Republican cosponsors, including Rep. Bill Huizenga, but no committee or floor action ever followed.

industries.note: The bill makes Medicare a reliable payer for stays beyond 190 lifetime days, bringing paying patients to psychiatric hospitals and specialty units. Patients benefit at the same time, since coverage continues instead of stopping mid-illness.
